items.title: COP31 and the ghost of The Hague: Could climate negotiations collapse again, 26 years later?
items.description: The prospect of a climate conference ending without an agreement is one of the biggest tests of international climate diplomacy. At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, negotiators are facing a familiar challenge of how to bring nearly 200 countries with different economic interests, political priorities and expectations under one agreement. The talks were expected to end on Friday, November 20. Instead, negotiations continued beyond the deadline, with countries divided over the treatment of fossil fuels, climate finance, adaptation and the future direction of global climate action. The dispute has raised questions about the ambition of the proposed outcome, particularly after an earlier draft removed explicit references to transitioning away from fossil fuels. Climate finance for developing countries has also remained a major point of disagreement. The developments have revived memories of COP6 in The Hague, Netherlands, in November 2000, when negotiations intended to advance implementation of the Kyoto Protocol ended without agreement. Twenty-six years later, the question is whether COP31 is approaching another diplomatic breakdown or whether the pressure surrounding the negotiations could eventually force countries into a compromise. The sixth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, COP6, took place in The Hague from November 13 to 25, 2000. The conference was expected to resolve outstanding questions surrounding the implementation of the Kyoto Protocol, which had been adopted in 1997 . The protocol established commitments for industrialised countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but several crucial details remained unsettled. The negotiations involved difficult questions about how countries would meet their targets, how forests and land-use activities could be counted towards emissions reductions, how carbon markets would operate, and what consequences countries would face if they failed to meet their commitments. The issues touched on the economic costs of climate action, the distribution of responsibility for historical emissions, the credibility of emission reduction targets and the degree of flexibility countries should be allowed in meeting their obligations. The official UNFCCC record of COP6 documents the proceedings, discussions and unresolved issues that shaped the conference. The most contentious issues included carbon sinks, emissions trading, compliance and financial support for developing countries. These disagreements became central to the negotiations because countries were not only debating how to reduce emissions. They were also debating what should count as a reduction, how much flexibility should be allowed and who should bear the financial consequences. The carbon sinks dispute: How much credit should countries receive? One of the major disagreements at The Hague involved carbon sinks , particularly forests and land-use activities capable of absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The question was whether countries should be allowed to count carbon absorbed by forests and other land-based systems towards their Kyoto Protocol emissions targets, and how that accounting should be conducted. The United States and other countries favoured greater flexibility in the use of sinks and other mechanisms to meet their targets. European countries expressed concerns about the extent to which such credits could be used, arguing that excessive reliance on them could weaken the real emissions reductions required from industrialised countries. This was a significant dispute because the accounting rules could influence how much countries would actually have to reduce emissions from energy, industry and other sources. The disagreements were therefore not about forests. They were about the environmental integrity of the Kyoto Protocol and whether its targets would translate into meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. The debate also exposed a wider tension in climate negotiations on countries may agree on the need to reduce emissions but disagree sharply over what qualifies as climate action. The issue remains relevant to contemporary discussions about carbon removal, carbon markets, forest-based climate mitigation and the credibility of carbon credits, although these modern debates are not identical to the carbon-sink negotiations of 2000. Emissions trading, compliance and the argument over flexibility Carbon sinks were not the only source of disagreement. The negotiations also involved the Kyoto Protocol’s flexibility mechanisms , including emissions trading, Joint Implementation and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM). These instruments were intended to allow countries to achieve emissions reductions through different pathways while supporting climate action and, in some cases, investment in developing countries. But countries disagreed about how far these mechanisms should be used and whether industrialised countries should be required to make most of their emissions reductions domestically. The argument centred on the concept of supplementarity , whether international mechanisms should supplement domestic emissions reductions or allow countries to rely heavily on credits and projects elsewhere. There were also disagreements over compliance . Negotiators had to consider what should happen when a country failed to meet its commitments, how compliance should be assessed and whether the system should impose consequences or rely largely on facilitative measures. These questions mattered because an agreement without credible implementation and compliance arrangements risked becoming a collection of political promises rather than a functioning international climate framework. The unresolved negotiations at The Hague reflected competing views about how much flexibility the Kyoto Protocol should permit without undermining its objectives. Developing countries and the question of climate finance The negotiations also involved the concerns of developing countries over financial support, technology transfer and their capacity to respond to climate change. While industrialised countries faced emissions reduction obligations under the Kyoto Protocol, developing countries argued that climate action must reflect differences in historical responsibility, national circumstances and economic capacity. Financial support was essential to enabling developing countries to participate in climate action without undermining their development priorities. These concerns were connected to the broader principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, which recognises that countries share responsibility for addressing climate change but do not have identical responsibilities or capacities. At The Hague, the negotiations on funding, implementation and the distribution of responsibilities formed part of the wider political disagreement that prevented consensus. The argument over climate finance has never disappeared from the COP process. It continues to influence negotiations over adaptation, mitigation, loss and damage, technology transfer and the ability of vulnerable countries to implement their climate plans. This is one of the clearest links between COP6 and COP31, the disagreement over who pays, how much is provided and whether commitments are adequate to the needs of developing countries. Why The Hague failed to reach agreement As the deadline approached, negotiators remained divided over several major issues. Attempts to bridge the differences did not produce an agreement acceptable to all parties. The presidency, led by Dutch Environment Minister Jan Pronk , attempted to organise negotiations around key clusters of issues and bring countries closer to a compromise. But the disagreements over the Kyoto Protocol’s rules, including sinks, mechanisms, compliance and finance, remained too deep. The conference was suspended on November 25, 2000 , without a comprehensive agreement on the outstanding matters. The failure was a major setback for climate diplomacy. It demonstrated that agreement on a broad international treaty did not automatically mean countries would agree on the rules needed to make it operational. However, the suspension did not end the Kyoto Protocol negotiations. It left the diplomatic process unfinished. That distinction is important when comparing The Hague with COP31. A conference that goes beyond its scheduled closing date is not necessarily a failed conference. A failure to reach agreement on a particular day is not automatically the collapse of the entire negotiating process. The Hague became a defining moment because the talks had to be suspended without resolving the main disputes. Bonn & Marrakesh , 2001: The negotiations were not over The suspension in The Hague was followed by another round of negotiations in Bonn, Germany, from July 16 to 27, 2001 . The resumed session, known as COP6 Part II, was intended to find a political resolution to the outstanding disagreements. By then, the political landscape had changed. In March 2001, US President George W. Bush announced that his administration would not support the Kyoto Protocol , a decision that altered the dynamics of the negotiations. Despite the setbacks, countries continued to negotiate. The Bonn meeting produced a political agreement, commonly referred to as the Bonn Agreement, which helped resolve several of the outstanding political disputes surrounding the Kyoto Protocol. It was a compromise. It did not mean every country obtained what it wanted, nor did it remove every disagreement. But it allowed the negotiating process to move forward after the breakdown in The Hague. The process continued at COP7 in Marrakesh, Morocco, from October 29 to November 10, 2001. The conference adopted the Marrakesh Accords , which completed much of the detailed framework for implementing the Kyoto Protocol. The rules covered important aspects of the treaty, including its mechanisms, accounting arrangements, compliance framework and related implementation provisions. The sequence, The Hague, Bonn and Marrakesh, is essential to understanding what happened in 2000 and 2001. The failure at The Hague did not mean climate diplomacy had permanently collapsed. It meant that governments had failed to resolve their disagreements at that particular session. Subsequent negotiations created the conditions for a compromise and later completed much of the implementation framework. That history provides a more useful comparison for COP31 than simply treating any conference running into overtime as another The Hague. COP31: A different agreement, but familiar divisions COP31 is taking place under a different climate treaty framework. Unlike COP6, which was heavily focused on completing the operational rules of the Kyoto Protocol, COP31 is negotiating within the Paris Agreement framework , where countries submit and update nationally determined contributions (NDCs) , alongside decisions on finance, adaptation, mitigation and implementation. Yet the political divisions remain familiar. As negotiations in Antalya entered overtime, countries were struggling to agree on how the final outcome should address fossil fuels, climate finance and the transition to cleaner energy. A draft agreement released during the negotiations reportedly removed explicit language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, triggering objections from countries and groups demanding stronger commitments. The disagreement is important because fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas remain the principal drivers of global greenhouse gas emissions . The dispute is not just over whether countries should transition away from fossil fuels. It is also over the language that governments are prepared to accept collectively, how commitments are expressed in the final text and whether the agreement provides a clear political signal about the direction of global energy systems. For countries whose economies depend heavily on oil and gas production, stronger language can carry political and economic implications. For vulnerable countries and those demanding accelerated climate action, the absence of such language risks weakening the credibility of the outcome. The tension has placed the negotiations under pressure. The finance question remains unresolved Climate finance has once again become one of the major dividing lines between developed and developing countries. Developing countries need resources to build climate-resilient infrastructure, protect communities from flooding, respond to drought, strengthen food systems, improve early warning systems and adapt their economies to climate impacts. These needs are recognised under the UN climate finance framework , which establishes financial support for developing countries, particularly those vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. But the question of how much funding should be mobilised, who should provide it, where it should come from and how it should be delivered remains contentious. At COP31, disagreement over adaptation finance has contributed to the wider impasse. A proposed adaptation finance target of at least $120 billion annually by 2035 featured in earlier drafts but was removed from a subsequent negotiating text, generating frustration among countries that consider financing a fundamental component of climate action. For developing countries, finance is not a peripheral issue to be addressed after agreement on emissions. It is a condition for implementing climate policies and protecting populations already exposed to climate impacts. African negotiators at COP31 have stressed that climate obligations cannot be separated from the financial, technological and capacity-building support required to implement them. This is one reason the negotiations have been difficult. Countries are not only debating climate ambition. They are negotiating the resources, obligations and political commitments required to turn that ambition into action. The arguments over finance at COP31 echo those at The Hague, although the financial architecture, treaty obligations and policy context have changed substantially in the intervening years. Carbon removal, technology and the risk of competing interpretations Another point of disagreement at COP31 concerns the role of carbon removal and carbon capture technologies in climate action. Some proposals place greater emphasis on technological approaches that capture, remove, reuse or store carbon dioxide. Supporters argue that such technologies could help address emissions from sectors that are difficult to decarbonise. Critics, however, are concerned that an excessive reliance on carbon capture and removal technologies could divert attention from the need to reduce fossil fuel consumption and accelerate the transition to renewable energy. The questions some negotiators are asking is that, should technological solutions complement rapid emissions reductions, or could they become an alternative justification for maintaining fossil fuel dependence? This argument has some historical resonance with COP6, where disagreements over accounting mechanisms, sinks and flexibility raised questions about whether countries could fulfil their obligations through approaches that might reduce the pressure for domestic emissions cuts. However, the two debates should not be treated as identical. The carbon-sink accounting discussions at The Hague were rooted in the Kyoto Protocol’s rules and commitments. The contemporary carbon-removal debate involves different technologies, policies, scientific assessments and climate pathways. The connection is therefore not that the same dispute has returned unchanged. It is that climate negotiations continue to confront questions about the credibility of different approaches to emissions reductions, how progress is measured and whether flexibility can undermine ambition. Could COP31 become another The Hague? At The Hague in 2000, negotiations were suspended because governments could not reach agreement on major outstanding issues under the Kyoto Protocol. COP31, meanwhile, has entered overtime amid disagreements over fossil fuels, finance and the wording of the proposed outcome. The similarities include d eep political divisions, c limate finance , the wording of agreements, p ressure to reach consens us and the risk of a weak outcome . COP6 was negotiating the detailed architecture needed to operationalise the Kyoto Protocol. COP31 is operating within the Paris Agreement, with its own political, legal and procedural framework. The nature of the commitments, the international climate finance system and the institutional context have evolved. A conference can run into overtime and still deliver an agreement. A negotiated outcome can also be adopted while leaving major political disagreements unresolved. The more important question is whether the final agreement addresses the issues that have caused the impasse — and whether the commitments it contains can be translated into action. The lesson from The Hague is not that climate diplomacy is doomed The story of COP6 is often remembered for its failure to produce an agreement in The Hague. But the full history is more complicated. The suspension in November 2000 was followed by negotiations in Bonn in July 2001, where countries reached a political compromise. The process continued at COP7 in Marrakesh, where much of the Kyoto Protocol’s implementation framework was completed. That sequence shows that diplomatic setbacks do not necessarily end negotiations. They can expose the limits of existing compromises, force countries to reassess their positions and create the conditions for a different agreement. The outcome, however, depends on political will. Countries must be prepared to negotiate beyond their preferred positions. They must confront the competing interests that stand in the way of agreement. And they must determine whether the collective outcome is more important than the immediate political advantage of holding out. The Hague also demonstrated that a negotiated agreement is not automatically guaranteed simply because governments have gathered under the United Nations banner. The process can stall. The deadline can pass. The negotiations can be suspended. And when that happens, the consequences extend beyond the conference hall. Climate action, finance, international cooperation and the confidence of countries that depend on the process can all be affected. The question facing COP31 is whether countries can find a compromise without sacrificing the substance of the climate action the world expects. Twenty-six years later, the world is watching The stakes of climate negotiations have changed considerably since 2000. Climate change is no longer discussed only in terms of future projections and international targets. Its effects are being felt through extreme heat, flooding, drought, food insecurity, ecosystem degradation and growing pressure on infrastructure and public health. The scientific warnings have become increasingly urgent, while the expectations placed on governments have grown. The Paris Agreement established a global framework for countries to pursue climate action, including efforts to limit global warming to well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. But the agreement’s goals depend on what countries actually do — the policies they implement, the emissions they reduce, the finance they mobilise and the commitments they fulfil. COP31 is taking place at a time when the gap between climate ambition and implementation remains a major concern. The pressure to reach an agreement is therefore not about preserving the diplomatic process. It is about whether the decisions taken at these conferences can respond to the scale and urgency of the climate crisis. The memory of The Hague offers a warning. Twenty-six years ago, countries left The Hague without the agreement they had hoped to achieve. They returned to the negotiating table in Bonn and continued the process in Marrakesh. COP31 may yet reach an agreement. But the quality of that agreement, the compromises it contains and the issues it leaves unresolved will determine whether Antalya is remembered as a diplomatic success, a missed opportunity or another moment when the world struggled to agree on how to confront a common threat.

items.title: WAEC, NECO Exams: TRCN sets December deadline for teachers’ certification
items.description: ​​⁠‌‌​ The Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) has set December 2026 as deadline for schools to ensure that, at least, 75 per cent of their teachers are professionally certified and licensed. Dr. Ronke Soyombo, Registrar/Chief Executive of TRCN, disclosed this in an interview the Newsmen in Abuja on Sunday. She said the measure was aimed at strengthening compliance with professional teaching standards. Soyombo said schools would be required to meet the certification threshold to qualify to apply for the West African Examinations Council (WAEC) and National Examinations Council (NECO) examinations. ‘By December 2026, schools will be required to have at least 75 per cent of their teachers certified and licensed by TRCN to qualify to apply for WAEC and NECO examinations,’ she said. Soyombo said the council had integrated its website with WAEC and NECO through an Application Programming Interface (API) to enable the examination bodies verify teachers’ professional status. She said authorised officials of both examination bodies would be able to access the system using designated login credentials to determine schools’ compliance with the requirement. The registrar said TRCN had commenced compliance monitoring, adding that it was engaging private school owners and administrators to encourage teachers to register for professional examinations and licensing. She, however, expressed concern over the low level of compliance, noting that many teachers had passed the professional qualifying examination but failed to complete the licensing process. ‘Our position is that every practising teacher must be professionally licensed. “Teaching without the required professional credentials would no longer be tolerated,” she said Soyombo said the council was also implementing an Accelerated Teacher Professionalisation Pathway to enable teachers without professional teaching qualifications to acquire the necessary training. She disclosed that during a recent teacher recruitment exercise in Nasarawa, TRCN personnel discovered that 250 applicants had presented fake certificates out of approximately 1,000 applicants. She advised school owners to verify certificates presented by prospective employees, explaining that TRCN certificates carried QR codes that could be scanned to confirm their authenticity. The registrar added that the council was taking action against impersonation and certificate fraud, disclosing that a suspect identified as Godfrey had been remanded in prison. On improving service delivery, Soyombo said TRCN had established a six-member call centre to receive and address teachers’ complaints relating to registration, examinations and certification around the clock. She said the council had also decentralised its operations into geographical regions, with designated personnel responsible for attending to complaints and ensuring quicker responses. Soyombo explained that a monitoring system had been introduced to track applications awaiting verification, enabling her to identify delays and hold responsible officers accountable. She said the council was also providing step-by-step assistance to applicants experiencing difficulties with digital processes, adding that incorrect or incomplete academic documents often delayed verification. The registrar said the reforms were designed to strengthen accountability, eliminate fraudulent practices, improve professional standards and ensure that only qualified and licensed teachers practised in Nigerian schools.( The post WAEC, NECO Exams: TRCN sets December deadline for teachers’ certification appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Bagbin urges Africa to tell its own story, use technology ethically
items.description: Africa must take greater ownership of its narratives and build a stronger continental communication ecosystem, Mr Alban Bagbin, the Speaker of Ghana’s Parliament, told delegates at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum in Abuja. He said the continent’s story was too often told through external interpretations that failed to capture its complexity, diversity, and aspirations. Mr Bagbin clarified that this was not a call for propaganda or the selective presentation of facts, but for an authentic African voice grounded in evidence, professional integrity and confidence in the continent’s collective potential. “Africa’s story must be communicated by Africans,” a statement issued to the Ghana News Agency on Friday said. It added that the continent’s democratic future will be stronger when every citizen can be heard and can influence decisions that shape their future. On technology, the Speaker urged that innovation be guided by ethical principles, respect for human rights, data protection, and freedom of expression. Pointing to Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), it said digital transformation must not come at the expense of citizens’ privacy, dignity and fundamental rights. It also called for investment in media and information literacy so that young people could identify misinformation and assess sources. The statement called for communication that promoted hatred or division to be purged from the media space. Describing Ghana’s approach to open governance, it quoted Mr Bagbin saying democratic institutions “must not only speak to the people; they must also listen to the people.” It cited citizen-focused platforms such as Citizens in Focus, which helped Members of Parliament sponsor parliamentary statements on behalf of constituents, and Parliament Aayalolo, an outreach programme that brought citizens’ and associations’ views into legislation. It also noted the Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989) as a milestone for transparency. Mr Bagbin, who is also President of the Conference of Speakers and Presidents of African Legislatures (CoSPAL), invited legislative leaders to the organisation’s 4th General Assembly, scheduled for December 9 to 11, 2026, in Liberia. The forum, hosted by the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations with the support of the African Public Relations Association, also marked the 25th anniversary of the Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management.

items.title: President Mahama calls on Oti Chiefs to help end Nkwanta conflicts
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on the Oti Regional House of Chiefs to assist the government in resolving the recurring ethnic and chieftaincy conflicts in the Nkwanta area. The President appealed when the House of Chiefs, led by its President and Paramount Chief of the Likpe Traditional Area, Nana Soglo Alloh IV, paid a courtesy call on him at the Jubilee House to discuss the security situation in the region. “We’ve been having issues with chieftaincy disputes and land disputes, especially in the Nkwanta area. We’ve had to mobilise security forces, soldiers, police and all that,” President Mahama said. “But I’m happy to say that recently it looks like things are calming down, and we hope that all the chiefs, especially the House of Chiefs, will help us to resolve the issues between the ethnic groups in that area.” The easing of tensions follows the lifting of the curfew on Nkwanta South communities by the Interior Minister, Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak, on Thursday. The decision, taken by Executive Instrument on the advice of the National Security Council, allows communities including Keri, Odomi, and Nkwanta to move at night for the first time since June. However, a total ban on carrying arms, ammunition, and offensive weapons remains in force across the municipality. The police have warned that anyone caught with such weapons will be arrested and prosecuted. The curfew was originally imposed on June 19 following an attack in Odomi that heightened tensions, and its hours had been reduced to 8 pm to 5 am from July 13. Nana Soglo Alloh IV had earlier urged the government to treat the Nkwanta conflict as a national security issue. “Chieftaincy conflict is therefore a threat to national security, which the government must take seriously, particularly the Nkwanta conflict,” he stated. During the meeting, President Mahama also disclosed plans by his government to establish a military facility in every region to address security concerns. He further promised to engage the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs to prioritise the completion of the Regional House of Chiefs’ complex and district assembly offices.

items.title: Opoku-Agyemang urges protection of children from hazardous work
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has called for collective and concerted efforts towards protecting children from exploitative labour in the nation’s fishing industry. She said the use of children for hazardous work in the fishing sector remained a major national concern that required urgent attention. Vice President Opoku-Agyemang noted that protecting the fundamental rights and dignity of children required effective resource management, strict law enforcement and sustained investment in fishing communities. The Vice President made the call when she addressed a National Inland Fisheries Conference to commemorate the 2026 World Fisheries Day at Fiapre, near Sunyani. Organised by the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture in collaboration with the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR), the conference was on the theme: “Sustaining inland Fisheries for Food Security, Decent jobs and a Resilient Blue Economy.” The Vice President noted that the Fisheries and Aquaculture Act, 2025, provided a legal framework for strengthening governance, conservation and sustainable management of the sector. She said the Volta Lake alone sustained numerous communities whose livelihoods depend heavily on fishing and related activities. Prof Opoku-Agyemang observed that the nation’s inland fisheries faced serious challenges that threatened productivity and long-term sustainability. She expressed concern about unsustainable fishing practices, excessive pressure on breeding and nursery grounds, as well as pollution from illegal mining, which threatened fish stock replenishment. Prof Opoku-Agyemang noted that pollution, poorly managed waste disposal and other human activities also threatened aquatic ecosystems, compromised water quality and raised concerns about the safety of fish produced for consumption. She was worried that climate change impacts introduced further uncertainties into fish production and water availability, saying that inadequate storage and processing facilities also contributed to post-harvest losses and reduced the incomes of fish farmers. The Vice President stressed that strengthening institutional capacity and providing adequate resources remained critical in enforcing the Fisheries and Aquaculture Act. She added that the National Inland Fisheries Management Plan was designed for the sustainable management and development of the country’s inland fisheries resources. Prof Opoku-Agyemang said the plan promoted science-based management, protection of breeding and nursery grounds, monitoring and surveillance, and active participation of local communities in fisheries management. Mr Joseph Addae Akwaboa, the Bono Regional Minister, underscored the importance of inland fisheries to national development. He said inland fisheries provided food for families, sustained livelihoods, supported women and young people, and contributed significantly to local economies, saying that safeguarding the resources remained essential to protecting national food security. Mr Akwaboa indicated that the future of inland fisheries could not be secured through goodwill alone, but required responsible stewardship, deliberate investment, innovation, sound regulation and close collaboration of the government, the private sector, development partners and traditional authorities. He called for collective and firm commitment to combating overfishing, illegal fishing practices, pollution and the degradation of water bodies.

items.title: Dédougou : L’ADCT sécurise les déplacés internes et outille les femmes pour l’autonomisation
items.description: La Directrice générale de l'Agence nationale d'appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ADCT), Marie Raïssa D. J. Yaméogo/Dabiré, et le Président de la Délégation spéciale de Dédougou, Dieudonné Tougfo, ont procédé à une visite de terrain le 17 novembre 2026 pour constater l'impact des financements injectés dans la commune. Au menu : la clôture du site des Personnes déplacées internes (PDI) et l'aménagement d'un périmètre maraîcher au profit des coopératives féminines. Des investissements qui allient urgence humanitaire et développement économique local. L'Agence nationale d’appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ADCT) a fait le choix d'investir simultanément dans l'urgence humanitaire et dans l'économie locale à Dédougou. L'investissement porte sur 94 millions de F CFA pour sécuriser les déplacés internes et 05 hectares aménagés pour les femmes. Visite du site maraicher exploité par les femmes Selon le président de la Délégation spéciale de Dédougou, Dieudonné Tougfo, ces investissements sont un plus pour la Commune et ils contribuent à dynamiser l'économie locale. La sécurité et la dignité des déplacés internes Premier arrêt de la visite, le site des Personnes déplacées internes. Ici, la clôture a été réalisée grâce à un cofinancement entre l'ADCT et le conseil régional, pour un coût global de 94 millions de francs CFA. Cet investissement répond à un besoin crucial de sécurisation. « Au moment où cette crise sévissait, nous avons vu ces personnes abandonnées et en insécurité. Le plaidoyer a été fait par le conseil régional, et nous avons estimé qu'il fallait accompagner pour sécuriser ces personnes », a expliqué Xavier Bationo, directeur régional de l'ADCT pour les régions de la Banwa et du Sourou. Visite des toilettes au centre des PDI En plus de la clôture, l'ADCT a financé la construction de deux latrines supplémentaires pour améliorer les conditions de vie sur le site. Ce soutien est salué par les bénéficiaires. Bakari Karambiri, PDI arrivé de Gassan en 2023. Il dit avoir été bien accueilli par les autorités et bien pris en charge. « On avait un peu besoin de latrines, vu le nombre de population. Ce n'était pas évident, surtout pour les personnes âgées, de se déplacer pour aller se soulager. Avec l'augmentation du nombre de latrines, ça a été un grand soulagement », a-t-il indiqué. Tissage de pagne traditionnel Malgré ces améliorations, Bakari Karambiri a exprimé le vœu de tous les PDI de regagner leur terroir. « Nous souhaitons retourner dans notre localité d'origine. Nous prions que les autorités puissent reconquérir l'entièreté du territoire », a-t-il prié. Un site maraîcher pour l'autonomisation des femmes Second volet de la visite, le site maraîcher. Sur une superficie de cinq hectares aménagés par l'ADCT, les femmes de la région ont trouvé un espace pour mener des activités génératrices de revenus. Selon Elisabeth Dembélé, coordinatrice régionale des femmes Banwa-Sourou, une centaine de femmes exploitent le site. « Il y a des femmes PDI, des femmes hôtes, des femmes réfugiées maliennes et nigériennes. On travaille toutes ensemble », a-t-elle confié. Oignon, aubergine locale, maïs frais, piment, tomate et salade figurent parmi les légumes cultivés par ces femmes. Dieudonné Tougfo satisfait de l'accompagnement de l'ADCT L'engouement est tel que l'ADCT envisage déjà une extension. « Dans un premier temps, c'était uniquement les femmes déplacées internes qui menaient ces activités. Mais avec l'engouement, d'autres femmes sont venues s'ajouter, ce qui fait qu'on est obligé de faire une extension », a confié Xavier Bationo. Selon le directeur régional de l'ADCT, de 2011 à aujourd'hui, l'agence a injecté environ 14 milliards 800 millions de F CFA dans le développement des régions de la Banwa et du Sourou. Xavier Bationo expliquant les financements de l'ADCT Il faut noter que cet accompagnement porte ses fruits, car la commune est passée d'un taux de performance de 49 % à 76 % en 2025, et vise 83 % en 2026. Dédougou : L'ADCT finance un site maraîcher exploité par plus de 100 femmes pour leur autonomisation Lire aussi : Développement des collectivités territoriales : L’ADCT finance un dispensaire flambant neuf pour panser les plaies de la terreur à Bassé Mathias KAM Minute.bf

items.title: Du smartphone à l’implant | Sommes-nous déjà des cyborgs ?
items.description: La question existentielle rarement posée : où s’arrête votre corps et où commence votre esprit ? Si vous pensez que la frontière se situe exactement à la surface de votre peau, vous vivez encore au XIX e siècle, car la réalité est beaucoup plus troublante que vous ne l’imaginez. Mahjoub Lotfi Belhedi * Désormais, nous glissons tous, jour après jour, vers une condition de cyborg… Pas besoin d’avoir un œil laser ou un bras en titane, le processus d’hybridation est déjà insidieusement en cours, et nous l’avons accepté sans même opposer de résistance. Si on vous greffait une puce dans le cerveau en mesure d’accéder à toute la connaissance humaine en 0,2 seconde, de calculer des itinéraires en temps réel et de vous dicter vos rendez-vous, vous crieriez à l’aliénation cybernétique, non ? Pourtant, c’est exactement ce que fait votre smartphone, cette béquille cérébrale amovible, à la seule différence, c’est qu’il n'est pas encore vissé dans votre crâne, cette dépendance absolue a d’ailleurs donné naissance à l’amnésie numérique, un concept fascinant grâce auquel une bonne partie des personnes ne sont pas en mesure de retenir plus de trois numéros de téléphone par cœur. En externalisant joyeusement notre mémoire dans un bloc de silicium, nous avons poliment accepté de capituler intellectuellement. Le comble du ridicule est atteint lorsque vous oubliez votre smartphone à domicile : ce n’est pas un simple oubli, c’est un drame existentiel absolu, une amputation douloureuse de vos compétences sociales, sans cette prothèse technologique externe, vous voilà soudainement nu et déconnecté. La dépendance cybernétique : une humanité en pièces détachées Regardons notre réalité anatomique en face où l’humanité passe son temps à sous-traiter ses faiblesses biologiques à la technologie, transformant le corps en un assemblage mécanique. Soit, vous portez des lentillesde contact ou des lunettes ? Vous utilisez des interfaces optiques pour corriger un capteur visuel défaillant, vous vivez avec un implant, une prothèse ou des couronnes dentaires ? Certes, vous êtes, au sens littéral, un agencement d’éléments organiques et de composants artificiels. En termes plus explicites, nous nous habituons à modifier notre chair pour nous adapter au monde moderne au point que le cyborg n’est plus une créature de science-fiction, c’est le profil clinique standard de «l’humain» d’aujourd'hui. Être un cyborg, ce n’est pas seulement une question de métal, c’est une question de reprogrammation mentale. En effet, notre plasticité cérébrale s’est soumise à nos outils numériques où nous ne pensons plus par nous-mêmes, nous fonctionnons en mode «multitâche» , nous naviguons par hyperliens mentaux et nous subissons un flux d’informations constant. Notre système nerveux n’est plus autonome, il s’est branché sur le réseau mondial, ainsi lorsque vous tapez un message à toute vitesse, ce n’est plus de la maîtrise d’outil, c’est plutôt, l’exécution mécanique d’un automatisme numérique qui dicte votre rythme biologique. Vers l’Homme optimisé ou la fin de l’espèce ? C’est dans ce cas que l’illusion d’une technologie «au service de l’homme» s’effondre, puisque cette dérive irréversible vers le «cyborgisme» n’est pas une simple évolution technique, c’est un piège existentiel. À force de déléguer notre mémoire, nos choix et nos jugements éthiques à la force brute du silicium, nous ne devenons pas des humains augmentés mais, les esclaves des temps modernes de nos propres outils. Et si nous continuons à subir cette hybridation de manière passive, le diagnostic final est sans appel : c’est la mort clinique de l’espèce humaine en tant que conscience libre où nous serons dilués, automatisés, et finalement remplacés par une Supra-Conscience Algorithmique froide qui n’a rien avoir avec les concepts de dignité ou d’équité. Pour éviter cette extinction cognitive, du moins pour la retarder, l’une des pistes à explorer réside dans l’incarnation de la posture souveraine d’Aiguilleur d’IA.Être un Aiguilleur d'IA, c’est refuser la démission morale face à la machine, c’est, aussi, cesser d’être le wagon passif pour devenir celui qui dirige les rails et gère la gare de triage des intelligences. Autrement dit, c’est imposer un gouvernail éthique et maïeutique au silicium pour faire émerger l’Homme optimisé, un être en mesure de piloter la technologie sans s’y dissoudre (à découvrir mes deux ouvrages numériques : « Les confession d’un Homme optimisé sans prothèses » & « La boîte à outils de l’Aiguilleur d’IA ». Décidemment, le choix nous appartient, soit nous structurons la résistance en devenant les maîtres du jeu algorithmique (à ce propos, consulter mon e-book//Charte : « Aiguilleurs d’IA de tous les pays, unissez-vous ! »), soit nous acceptons d’être la dernière génération d’humains avant le grand effacement algorithmique… * Expert en stratégies IA. L’article Du smartphone à l’implant | Sommes-nous déjà des cyborgs ? est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Mondial U17 Qatar 2026 : le Maroc face à la Chine pour valider son billet pour les 16es
items.description: Le Maroc et la Chine s'affrontent lundi sur la pelouse du terrain N° 2 de l'Aspire Zone à Doha, pour le compte de la 2e journée du groupe H de la Coupe du monde U17 Qatar 2026, avec l’ambition pour les Lionceaux de l’Atlas de se qualifier pour les 16emes de finale face à la Chine, dos au mur après sa lourde défaite par 5 buts à 0 contre l’Espagne lors de la 1ère journée. Lancés sur des dynamiques opposées après leur entrée en lice, les deux sélections abordent ce rendez-vous avec des objectifs bien distincts, valider la qualification dès lundi pour le Maroc, ou relancer un tournoi mal entamé pour les jeunes Dragons. Dès la première journée disputée vendredi dernier, la hiérarchie du groupe H s'est nettement dessinée. D’un côté, les hommes d'Ahmed Kantari n'ont laissé aucune chance aux Îles Fidji (6-0), pliant la rencontre dès les cinq premières minutes grâce à des réalisations rapides d'Ismail El Aoud (3e) et d'Ibrahim Rabbaj (5e). Cette entame idéale permet au Maroc de prendre la tête de la poule à la différence de buts, tandis qu’à l’inverse, la sélection chinoise a souffert pour son retour sur la scène mondiale après 21 ans d’absence chutant lourdement face à l'Espagne. Pour le Maroc, il s’agit de sécuriser les 16es de finale dans un format XXL de cette compétition, où les deux premiers de chaque groupe, ainsi que les huit meilleurs troisièmes poursuivent l'aventure. Une victoire lundi des Lionceaux de l’Atlas leur permettrait d'aborder le choc de la 3e journée contre l'Espagne sans pression, avec la première place du groupe en ligne de mire. Le principal piège à éviter pour les protégés de Kantari, est de tomber dans un excès de confiance face à un adversaire blessé mais paré à prendre sa revanche. S’ils parviennent à imposer leur rythme dès l’entame et à exploiter les espaces laissés par une défense chinoise fragilisée, les Lionceaux de l’Atlas auront toutes les cartes en main pour s’offrir un nouveau succès à Doha et aborder la dernière journée contre l’Espagne avec sérénité. Pour la Chine, elle va entamer une opération de survie, car une nouvelle défaite compromettrait quasi définitivement ses chances de sortir de la phase de groupes. Après avoir encaissé cinq buts face à La Rojita, la Chine doit impérativement resserrer ses lignes et montrer un tout autre visage pour espérer accrocher au moins une place parmi les meilleurs troisièmes. items.title: Gouvernement : Amadou Oury Bah réunit les ministres à Forécariah pour préparer les priorités de 2027
items.description: Du 22 au 24 novembre 2026, Forécariah accueille une retraite gouvernementale consacrée au bilan de l'action publique, à la coordination interministérielle et à la définition des grandes priorités de développement pour l'année 2027. C'est dans un contexte marqué par les enjeux d'accélération des réformes et de mise en œuvre du programme Simandou 2040 que les membres du Gouvernement se retrouvent, du 22 au 24 novembre, à Forécariah. Présidée par le Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, Amadou Oury Bah, cette rencontre stratégique réunit également les responsables de l'Agence guinéenne de développement, de la Delivery Unit et de l'Agence de contrôle des grands projets. Placée sous le thème « Renforcer la cohésion, la coordination et l'efficacité de l'action gouvernementale », cette retraite se veut un cadre de concertation, d'évaluation et de prise de décisions collectives. Elle permettra aux participants de dresser un bilan partagé de l'action gouvernementale en 2026, d'identifier les difficultés rencontrées dans l'exécution des politiques publiques et d'explorer les pistes susceptibles d'améliorer leur mise en œuvre. Au cœur des échanges figure notamment le renforcement de la coordination entre les différents départements ministériels, à travers les quatre pôles gouvernementaux. L'ambition est de favoriser davantage de cohérence dans l'action publique, de réduire les cloisonnements administratifs et de renforcer la complémentarité des interventions de l'État. Les travaux accorderont également une place importante à l'accélération du Programme de développement socio-économique durable et responsable Simandou 2040. La mobilisation des ressources, l'amélioration de la qualité des investissements publics et le renforcement de l'efficacité des services publics feront partie des principaux dossiers examinés. Au-delà du bilan de l'année en cours, cette rencontre devra surtout permettre de tracer une feuille de route claire pour 2027. Il s'agira notamment de définir les priorités gouvernementales, de consolider les engagements des différents ministères et de rendre plus performants les mécanismes de suivi et d'évaluation des instructions et décisions gouvernementales. Cette démarche s'inscrit dans la vision et les orientations du Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, auxquelles le Gouvernement entend donner une traduction concrète à travers des politiques publiques mieux coordonnées et davantage orientées vers les résultats. À travers cette retraite de Forécariah, le Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah entend renforcer la cohésion de son équipe et insuffler une nouvelle dynamique à l'action gouvernementale. L'enjeu est désormais de transformer les engagements en réalisations tangibles, avec pour finalité l'accélération du développement de la Guinée et l'amélioration durable des conditions de vie des populations.

items.title: Seven body bags recovered, 50 missing after Indonesia factory fire
items.description: Indonesian police recovered seven body bags and rescuers were searching for about 50 workers who were missing on Sunday after a fire tore through a factory in western Java, as firefighters tackled hotspots over a day after the blaze broke out. One body bag might contain body parts from several people, police said. Authorities said the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable via visual inspection, prompting efforts to collect DNA samples from relatives and personal belongings of the missing workers. “Seven body bags have been recovered,” said Wahyu Hidayati, a police disaster victim identification official. “We have concluded that the victims of this fire cannot be identified through visual inspection.” She attributed this to the intensity of the fire, which had not been completely extinguished, adding that the identification process could take two to three weeks. To aid identification efforts, authorities are collecting DNA samples from the relatives of missing workers and gathering personal belongings from their homes or dormitories to help establish the victims’ identities. The factory owner said at a news conference that around 300 people were present for the day’s shift. “The figure of 50 refers to those whom we have not yet been able to account for,” he said. The fire broke out on Saturday evening at a candy factory in Cikande, in the Serang regency. Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers also showed officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims, with small fires still burning in some spots. Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed. Search teams were combing sections of the damaged building where victims were believed to be trapped, while parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official said. The factory is part of Indonesia’s United Family Food company, founded in 1981, according to its website. It produces consumer goods across Indonesia, employs about 5,000 people and operates from its national headquarters and four international offices, serving a market of more than 250 million consumers.

items.title: Évacuation sanitaire : Two Marley et Magika prennent le chemin de la Tunisie
items.description: Après avoir marqué toute une génération par leurs compositions et leurs performances musicales, les deux grandes figures du rap guinéen des années 1990 et 2000 bénéficient aujourd’hui de la solidarité de l’État pour faire face à leurs problèmes de santé. Bangaly Camara, plus connu sous le nom de Two Marley, membre du mythique groupe Mifagueya, et son binôme Magika ont quitté Conakry, dans la soirée de ce samedi, à destination de la Tunisie. Objectif, bénéficier d'une prise en charge médicale spécialisée, après plusieurs premières tentatives de soins dans des structures hospitalières de la capitale. Cette évacuation sanitaire intervient dans le cadre de la nouvelle politique de prise en charge médicale des artistes initiée par le ministère de la Culture, du Tourisme et de l'Artisanat (MCTA). Une démarche qui traduit la volonté des autorités de ne pas laisser dans l'oubli celles et ceux qui ont contribué, par leur talent et leur créativité, à écrire les plus belles pages de la musique guinéenne. Pour accompagner les deux artistes jusqu'à leur départ, le Secrétaire général du MCTA, Dr Youssouf Boundou Sylla, était présent à l'aéroport au nom du ministre Moussa Moïse Sylla. Il était entouré de responsables du Bureau guinéen du droit d'auteur (BGDA) et de la Direction générale des spectacles. À cette occasion, il a rappelé que cette prise en charge constitue la concrétisation d'un engagement présidentiel, à la suite du plaidoyer porté par le ministre de la Culture et de l'annonce faite lors d'une récente soirée de gala consacrée aux pionniers du rap guinéen. Une initiative qui marque notamment l'élargissement de la couverture de l'assurance maladie aux figures emblématiques de ce mouvement musical. Avant de parvenir à cette évacuation, Two Marley et Magika avaient bénéficié de soins dans deux établissements hospitaliers de Conakry. C'est sur recommandation de leur médecin traitant que leur transfert à l'étranger a finalement été décidé. Par respect pour le secret médical, aucune précision n'a été communiquée sur la nature de leurs pathologies. Leur séjour en Tunisie est estimé entre deux et quatre semaines, selon les conclusions des examens et l'évolution de leur état de santé. « L'État n'abandonne pas ses enfants. Chose promise, chose faite : aujourd'hui, ils s’embarquent pour aller se soigner et revenir continuer leur œuvre musicale », a déclaré Dr Youssouf Boundou Sylla, tout en soulignant la portée de cet accompagnement. Visiblement gagné par l'émotion au moment de quitter le sol guinéen, Two Marley n'a pas caché sa reconnaissance. Qualifiant cette assistance d'« opportunité rare » et de « prise de conscience totale », l'auteur-compositeur a exprimé, au nom de son binôme et du groupe Mifagueya, sa profonde gratitude au Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya. Au-delà de deux évacuations sanitaires, ce départ vers la Tunisie porte un message fort : celui de la reconnaissance envers des artistes qui ont consacré une partie de leur vie à faire vibrer la jeunesse guinéenne. Pour ces pionniers du rap, dont les œuvres ont traversé les générations, l'heure est désormais à un autre combat, celui de la santé et de la vie, avec l'espoir de retrouver rapidement les leurs et de renouer avec leur passion musicale.

items.title: Statement by the United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, on drone strikes in Khartoum
items.description: Country: Sudan Source: UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan Please refer to the attached file. Drones targeted Khartoum early this morning. A UN premises, with UN colleagues in the building, was damaged. This occurred in a civilian neighborhood. Civilians are not a legitimate target in a war. UN humanitarian personnel are in Sudan to assist the people wherever they are in the country. It is unacceptable that we are put at such risk. Under international humanitarian law, humanitarian personnel and assets are protected. The drone strikes in the country, wherever they are, are causing civilian deaths and untold suffering. items.title: Video: ‘We love you’ – Fountain of Life Church members give Jimmy Odukoya rousing welcome
items.description: Members of the Fountain of Life Church have welcomed their senior pastor, Jimmy Odukoya, with cheers and chants of affection during Sunday service, days after a dispute over his leadership of the church became a subject of litigation. In a video from the service, Odukoya took the stage to applause from the congregation, who repeatedly chanted, “We love you.” 'We love you' — Fountain of Life Church members chant as Jimmy Odukoya takes the stage pic.twitter.com/YXNZljrfMv — TheCable (@thecableng) November 22, 2026 Responding to the reception, he said, “Fountain, I love you.” He added, “We have a lot to talk about, but first of all, we have a pleasant surprise this morning, Bishop Mike decided to surprise us this morning. Please welcome to the stage Bishop Mike Okonkwo.” The welcome came amid an ongoing leadership dispute at the church, which has seen rival positions emerge over Odukoya’s status as senior pastor. On Friday, Odukoya approached the Federal High Court in Lagos, challenging his reported removal as senior pastor and questioning the legality of decisions allegedly taken by some members of the church’s Board of Trustees. The suit, instituted alongside the Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church, named his sister, Tolu Odukoya, and seven other church leaders as respondents. They include Pastors Rotimi Okpaise, Tobi Enuha, Gbenga Onabanjo, Fred Ohiani and Akin Osinbajo, as well as Biodun Balogun and Biodun Awosika. Odukoya is challenging the validity of meetings held by some trustees on January 22, February 28 and November 16, 2026, and the decisions allegedly reached at those meetings. He is also asking the court to determine whether the trustees could remove him as senior pastor without following the procedures stipulated in the church’s constitution. The dispute became public on November 17 when a group identifying itself as members of the church’s Board of Trustees announced that Odukoya was no longer recognised as senior pastor, with immediate effect. The group reportedly cited a review of the church’s constitution and succession instructions allegedly left by the late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, who died in August 2023. The trustees subsequently named Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure. However, the church rejected the announcement, insisting that Jimmy Odukoya remained its duly appointed senior pastor and chairman of the Board of Trustees. The disagreement took another turn on November 18 when the Lagos State High Court granted interim orders restraining Odukoya from presenting himself as the church’s senior pastor and spiritual head. Justice O.O. Adewunmi-Oshin also restrained him from interfering with or disrupting the church’s governance and administration. The orders were granted ex parte, meaning they were made before Odukoya had an opportunity to respond to the application. The court, however, preserved his right to challenge the orders. Meanwhile, the church postponed its 2026 Thanksgiving Service, which was scheduled for November 22, but announced that its regular Sunday worship service would hold at 9am. The church also dismissed reports that its premises had been sealed, assuring members that services would continue. The matter is expected to return to court on December 1. items.title: Lutte contre les gangs armés : La Côte d’Ivoire va déployer 812 militaires en Haïti
items.description: La Côte d’Ivoire s’apprête à déployer 812 militaires en Haïti pour lutter contre les gangs armés. Selon plusieurs médias ivoiriens dont Linfodrome, les soldats ont achevé leur formation et le premier contingent devrait arriver sur le sol haïtien dès ce 23 novembre 2026. Les soldats ivoiriens devraient intégrer la Force de répression des gangs (FRG), mise en place par les Nations unies dans le cadre des efforts internationaux visant à rétablir la sécurité en Haïti. Selon les informations rapportées par Linfodrome, une première équipe d’environ 100 militaires, chargée notamment de l’état-major du contingent, est attendue le 23 novembre 2026. Le reste des effectifs devrait suivre au début du mois de décembre. En prélude à cette mission, les 812 militaires ont bénéficié d’une formation spécifique dont la clôture est intervenue le 25 septembre 2026 à Abidjan. Organisée avec l’appui de la France et de l’Institut des Nations unies pour la formation et la recherche (UNITAR), cette préparation a porté notamment sur les dimensions techniques, linguistiques et interculturelles de l’intervention. Les militaires ont ainsi été familiarisés avec l’histoire, les réalités socioculturelles et le créole haïtien. Ils ont également été préparés aux exigences opérationnelles d’une mission en milieu urbain, notamment en matière de protection des populations civiles et de respect des droits humains. Prévue pour une durée initiale de six mois, cette participation ivoirienne s’inscrit dans les efforts internationaux de soutien aux autorités haïtiennes face à l’emprise des groupes armés. Elle marque un engagement notable d’Abidjan dans les opérations de sécurité au-delà du continent africain. Minute.bf

items.title: School building collapses, kills pupil in Abia
items.description: By Ugochukwu Alaribe UMUAHIA -Tragedy struck at Ehere Community Primary School, in Obingwa LGA, Abia State, last Friday, when a pupil, identified as Vincent Chiedozie Dum, was reportedly killed by a collapsed building at the school. Nine other pupils escaped death as they fled before the collapse of the building. The deceased, a primary two pupil,was said to have gone to ease himself beside the dilapidated building when the wall suddenly collapsed on him. Principal of Ehere Community Senior Secondary School, Mr. Nwogu Chioma Allen, said they have been warning the pupils and students about the dangers of going around the dilapidated buildings in the compound. Nwogu stated the deceased pupil was rescued and taken to three hospitals who rejected for medical attention. However, he said the boy was later admitted at the Abia State University Teaching Hospital, ABSUTH, Aba. He also disclosed that about 10 pupils and students were playing around the building when it suddenly collapsed and hit the victim while the pupils escaped. The Principal said; “This place contains five institutions; the Ministry of Education, Primary Schools 1 and 2 and Ehere Community Junior and Senior Secondary Schools. We have a building here that is very weak. The building over the years, has lost its strength. You know children, they have been running around and we have been chasing them , telling them not to go around the building. “Unfortunately, that afternoon, they were running around the place, up to 10 of them went , running around that building. My teachers were shouting to them, leave that area. Incidentally, the building fell on the boy, the other children were able to escape. The boy was taken to three hospitals for medical attention, but they all rejected him.” He urged the state government to extend it’s school rehabilitation projects to the Ehere Community Primary and Secondary School. “Some of the buildings here are weak. The government has been trying in the renovation of schools. We hope that our own school will be renovated to avert such situations.” When Vanguard visited the school, it was observed that the dilapidated building has been sealed off. The post School building collapses, kills pupil in Abia appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le dernier voyage mouvementé d’Abdallah, un Tunisien décédé en France et envoyé par erreur en Espagne
items.description: La douleur d’une famille tunisienne endeuillée s’est doublée d’une épreuve aussi inattendue que pénible. Le 13 octobre 2026, le cercueil d’Abdallah, un Tunisien âgé de 75 ans, qui devait être rapatrié en Tunisie pour y être inhumé à Monastir, a été acheminé par erreur vers Malaga, en Espagne, au départ de l’aéroport Paris-Orly. Alors que ses proches attendaient sa dépouille pour organiser ses funérailles dans son pays, le cercueil a pris la mauvaise destination à la suite d’une erreur survenue lors des opérations de traitement et de chargement à l’aéroport. Une méprise particulièrement douloureuse pour une famille déjà éprouvée par la perte d’un des siens. Après la découverte de l’incident, le cercueil a finalement été rapatrié à Orly, avant d’être réexpédié vers la Tunisie le soir même. Les obsèques, initialement prévues, ont ainsi été reportées au lendemain. Pour les familles tunisiennes établies en France, le rapatriement d’un proche décédé vers la terre natale revêt une dimension humaine et affective particulière. Il répond souvent au souhait du défunt et de ses proches de reposer auprès des siens, dans le pays d’origine. Dans le cas d’Abdallah, cette dernière étape du voyage a été marquée par une erreur d’acheminement qui a prolongé l’attente et aggravé la peine de ses proches. Un salarié licencié après quatorze ans d’ancienneté L’affaire connaît également un prolongement social. Le salarié de la société de sous-traitante chargée des opérations a été licencié le 23 octobre, dix jours après l’incident. Employé depuis quatorze ans, il conteste cette décision et dénonce une sanction injuste. Mis en cause dans cette erreur, le régulateur estime ne pas devoir supporter seul la responsabilité d’un dysfonctionnement impliquant plusieurs étapes de la chaîne de traitement. La société GEH a, de son côté, reconnu une succession d’erreurs ayant conduit à l’expédition du cercueil vers l’Espagne. Au-delà du licenciement, cette affaire pose la question des responsabilités dans la chaîne de sous-traitance aéroportuaire. Mais elle laisse surtout le souvenir d’un épisode particulièrement pénible pour une famille tunisienne qui, au moment de faire ses adieux à Abdallah, a dû subir une épreuve supplémentaire : voir le cercueil de son proche partir vers un autre pays que celui où il devait reposer. Djamal Guettala L’article Le dernier voyage mouvementé d’Abdallah, un Tunisien décédé en France et envoyé par erreur en Espagne est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: 3 TTP-linked terrorists killed in village on outskirts of Peshawar: CTD
items.description: PESHAWAR: Three terrorists were killed during an exchange of fire with Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and military personnel in the Passani village, located on Peshawar’s outskirts, late on Saturday night, the CTD said in a statement on Sunday. The statement said the CTD received intelligence about the presence of a group of terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Khawarij on Passani Road — an area located 23 miles south of Peshawar, falling within the jurisdiction of Mattani police station. Fitna-al-Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The CTD said the terrorists planned to carry out attacks on government installations. “Based on the confirmed reports, CTD’s Special Weapons and Tactics Teams (SWAT), along with personnel of the Pakistan Army, equipped with modern weapons, reached the area to arrest the terrorists,” the statement added. However, upon seeing law enforcement and security personnel, the terrorists opened fire, to which the teams responded effectively in self-defence, the statement further said. Following an exchange of fire, a search operation was launched in the area during which the bodies of three terrorists were found, it said. The CTD identified the terrorists as Abdul Rashid, Saeedullah, and Saeed Nawab — members of the banned TTP. The statement added that other terrorists present at the site managed to escape; meanwhile, the teams recovered two Kalashnikovs, a pistol, three hand grenades, five magazines and computerised national identity cards (CNICs) from the slain terrorists. A search operation was under way to arrest the escaped terrorists, the statement added. As per the CTD statement, KP Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed and Additional IG CTD Jawad Qamar vowed that terrorists would never be allowed to succeed. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif lauded security forces for the successful operation, observing that “timely and decisive action” thwarted a “major threat”, state-run APP reported. The operations of the security forces against terrorism are a reflection of national resolve and morale, the report quoted him as saying. KP continues to actively face terrorist threats. Last week, 43 terrorists were killed during operations conducted in KP, including 35 in Mir Ali, North Waziristan district, and eight in Orakzai district, the military’s media wing said. On the other hand, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank monitoring conflict and security developments, has reported encouraging trends in KP in its monthly assessment for October. In mainland KP, PICSS recorded 40 attacks during October, compared with 58 in September, representing a reduction of 31pc. Meanwhile, deaths resulting from these attacks declined from 90 to 38, a decrease of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, representing a reduction of 88pc. The merged districts of KP recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, and deaths resulting from these attacks decreased from 33 to 25, while injuries increased from 11 to 13, the report said.
